newsitem.title: INDIA: India's "fodder" scandal is a decade-long saga.
newsitem.headline: India's "fodder" scandal is a decade-long saga.

text.p: A $280 million scandal, which sparked the resignation of a powerful Indian political leader on Friday and rocked Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's coalition for weeks, stretches back more than a decade.

Laloo Prasad Yadav, chief minister of the eastern state of Bihar, resigned on Friday following a court order seeking his arrest, which was later stayed by the Supreme Court to which he had moved an appeal to avoid arrest.

Bihar authorities ordered raids on the offices of the Animal Husbandry Department in January last year after officers discovered what appeared to be excessive withdrawals from the state treasury over a period extending into the mid-1980s.
The state government set up a one-man judicial commission on March 10 last year to probe the "fodder scam", which acquired its tag from the alleged embezzlement of animal welfare funds.
One day later, the state high court ordered the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), India's federal police force, to investigate the matter.
The CBI questioned Laloo Prasad Yadav, Bihar chief minister and then head of Gujral's Janata Dal party, on January 6 this year.
Earlier the agency had interrogated then junior rural areas and employment minister Chandradeo Prasad Varma as well as Jagannath Mishra, a former Bihar chief minister and a Congress party leader.
The CBI said in April it had decided to prosecute Yadav -- known in India simply as Laloo -- as well as Varma, Mishra and 53 others. Yadav, Varma and Mishra have said they are innocent.
The governor of Bihar on June 17 authorised the CBI to prosecute all three leaders. Varma resigned three days later.
Following differences over party elections in Janata Dal, Yadav formed his breakaway Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD) earlier this month.

Various members of Gujral's 15-party coalition, the main opposition Bharatiya Janata Party and the United Front government's powerful ally, the Congress party, had repeatedly urged Yadav to step down and face legal action.
The ruling United Front has been debating whether to admit the RJD into its fold because of Yadav's refusal to resign following his indictment by federal police in the scandal.
Yadav resigned after a court in Bihar's capital, Patna, ordered his arrest. The Supreme Court later said he could not be detained until it had heard his plea against detention.
